title: How to Build Voice Agents That Don't Fall Apart When You Interrupt - Jesse Hall, LiveKit
talk_summary: A LiveKit talk on building real-time voice agents that survive interruptions, arguing that latency is a fixed budget (500-600ms ideal, ~1.5s tolerable) and that you must evaluate whole conversations with simulated users rather than picking models off leaderboards. The core transferable ideas are end-to-end stack benchmarking with identical inputs across model swaps, and measuring the user-perceived metric (time to first audio/sentence) rather than proxy metrics.

takeaways.technique: Personalized stack benchmark via model-swap loop
takeaways.what_they_do: They take one complete working agent, run identical simulated scenarios against it, then swap only the model(s) and rerun, building a private benchmark that ranks stacks for their actual use case rather than trusting public leaderboards.
takeaways.evidence_quote: We have the same agent, the same scenarios, but we change the models... Every model sees identical input byte for byte.
takeaways.numbers: Gemma 4 31B on LiveKit inference ranked highest for their hotel agent; same model on another provider was slower

takeaways.technique: Score outcomes AND process, not just completion
takeaways.what_they_do: They score the final state (did the correct reservation hit the DB) plus the trajectory (did it take 10 steps when 2 sufficed, did it hallucinate a tool call), because agents can game completions.
takeaways.evidence_quote: We don't score it based on just the completion alone... agents can game completions... Did they take 10 steps when they only should have taken two steps?

takeaways.what_they_do: Every observed failure becomes a permanent regression scenario that is rerun continuously, so the benchmark grows from real incidents.
takeaways.evidence_quote: when you find these failures, you turn those into regression scenarios and you keep testing over and over again

takeaways.technique: Measure user-perceived metric, not proxy metric
takeaways.what_they_do: They reject time-to-first-byte and time-to-first-token as misleading and measure time-to-first-audio and time-to-first-sentence, because a byte or token isn't what the user experiences.
takeaways.evidence_quote: a byte does not equal audio... time to first audio is what we should be measuring, not time to first byte
takeaways.numbers: Providers shipping up to 3/4 second of silence after first byte; 210ms TTFB looked fast but wasn't

takeaways.technique: Decouple slow tool calls from the conversation thread
takeaways.what_they_do: An async await on the tool call hands control back so the agent keeps working/talking while a slow backend operation runs, instead of blocking on it.
takeaways.numbers: Backend tool calls cited at 2-40+ seconds

takeaways.technique: Latency budget as a fixed window to fit work into
takeaways.what_they_do: They frame end-to-end latency as a finite budget and ask 'how much capability can I fit inside it' rather than 'how fast can each part go'.
takeaways.evidence_quote: The answer is how human-like of an agent can I fit within this latency window.
takeaways.numbers: 500-600ms feels human; ~1.5s starts to feel off
